title: Lambdas as commands, and Command against Strategy

questions.stem: `history.executeCommand(() -> { counter.incrementAndGet(); })` is rejected by the compiler when `executeCommand` takes the page's `Command` interface. Why?

options.text: A lambda can implement an abstract class, but not an interface type.
options.says: Runnable and Consumer are interfaces, and the page passes lambdas for them as commands; the target type being an interface is not the problem.

options.text: A lambda is accepted for Runnable, Consumer or Callable parameters, not custom ones.
options.says: Any interface with a single abstract method is functional, so a custom one-method command interface would take a lambda too.

options.text: Its target type has three abstract methods, so one lambda body cannot supply them.
options.says: A lambda needs a functional interface, one abstract method; a Command with three of them needs a class such as the page's LambdaCommand wrapper.

questions.stem: Per the page's comparison, how does a command differ from a strategy?

options.text: A command has one method for its holder to call, which a strategy lacks.
options.says: A strategy also exposes a method its context calls, such as sort(data); having a method to call is common to both.

options.text: A command holds a reference to the receiver it acts on, set when it is built.
options.says: A command binds to its receiver, like an InsertCommand holding its editor, while a strategy works on whatever data it is passed.

options.text: A command holds no state of its own, so that it can be replayed later.
options.says: The page says the opposite: a command may hold mutable state for undo, and it is the strategy that should be stateless.
